analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional districts with independent commissions and bans mid-decade redraws.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor and died in the House Judiciary Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have taken congressional redistricting out of the hands of state legislators. It required every state to set up an independent commission to draw its congressional map, barred legislators' maps from considering party affiliation or where incumbents live, banned states from redrawing districts more than once per decade, and opened the whole process to the public with an online portal and hearings. If a commission's plan was rejected, the state's highest court — or a federal court — would pick or draw a replacement.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, whose congressional districts would be drawn without regard to party advantage or protecting incumbents, and who would get a transparent, public process instead of maps negotiated behind closed doors by the party in power in each statehouse.

how_it_helps.text: Each state must establish an independent redistricting commission to develop its congressional map, and the commission cannot consider party affiliation, voting history, or where incumbents live when drawing districts, except as needed to comply with the Voting Rights Act.

The bill bars a state from redrawing its congressional map more than once after each census, unless a court orders a redraw to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act — closing the door on mid-decade partisan redistricting.

Commission meetings must be public, the state must maintain a public website with census data, interactive mapping software, and a way for any citizen to submit a proposed map or comment, and the commission must hold public input meetings around the state before submitting a plan.

If a commission's plan is not enacted, the state's highest court may select a plan; if the court does not, a federal district court must develop one, so a map always gets drawn by someone barred from the legislature's process.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and the parties that control state legislatures, who lose the power to draw their own districts and their ability to lock in safe seats or maximize seats statewide. The bill also authorizes federal payments of $150,000 per congressional seat to fund the commissions.

drawbacks.text: The commission design is not fully independent: its members are appointed by the majority and minority leaders of each chamber of the state legislature, so the two major parties still choose the people drawing the map.

The bill overrides how states have historically drawn their own congressional districts under their own constitutions, a federalism objection that courts and state officials have raised about similar proposals, and it asserts federal authority under the Elections Clause and the Fourteenth Amendment in the bill's own findings.

The bill authorizes federal payments to states ($150,000 per House seat) to run the commissions, a new federal expense, and it applies only to congressional districts, leaving state legislative districts drawn by the same gerrymandering processes untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — maps drawn without regard to party or incumbent advantage, once per decade, in public — is significant for the fairness of House elections, and the cost is mostly borne by officeholders' power rather than by the public. The honest objections are that the commission is appointed by legislative leaders of both parties, that it imposes a federal uniform process on a task states have historically run themselves, and that it does nothing about gerrymandered state legislative districts.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, later referred to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen (D-TN) introduced the bill on July 1, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, but no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the parties that control state legislatures keep the power to draw congressional maps to their own advantage, including the ability to redraw districts mid-decade, which several states exercised in this period. Voters got no change in how maps are drawn.

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require independent redistricting commissions and ban mid-decade redistricting; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill; it sat from referral in July 2021 until a subcommittee referral in November 2022 and then died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities
against.role: Officeholders whose redistricting power the bill would have removed
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the bill's inaction; both parties drew maps to their advantage in the 2021 redistricting cycle and neither party's members cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, and it had no cosponsors from either party, so the only record of support is its single Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have barred map-drawers from considering where incumbents live and banned mid-decade redraws, ending the practice of drawing districts tailored to protect sitting members. The bill's death leaves incumbents' map-drawing protections intact.

Majority parties in statehouses currently draw congressional maps to maximize their party's seats; the bill would have moved that job to a commission and a court fallback. Both parties used this power in the 2021 cycle, which is the context in which the bill went nowhere.
The bill would have made the EAC the paying agency for state redistricting commissions, $150,000 per House seat. A modest administrative role, no conflict with the public interest.
